tiers.3: predict the effect & pick the drug

practice.stem: When does coronary perfusion mainly occur?
options: During systole, when the squeeze pushes blood into the coronaries
During atrial contraction, when the atria top off the ventricles
During diastole, when the relaxed muscle lets the coronaries fill
During isovolumetric contraction, when every valve is closed
practice.rationale: Coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole: "During systole, the constriction of the heart kind of prevents blood flow from going through the coronary vessels." The squeeze of systole (or the moment contraction starts) is exactly when the coronaries are pressed shut.

practice.stem: The client's angiogram shows the entire left anterior descending (LAD) artery is blocked. Which area of the heart is most at risk?
options: The anterior left ventricle and the anterior interventricular septum
The lateral wall of the left ventricle and portions of the left atrium
The right ventricle along with portions of the heart's conduction system
The right atrium only, since it holds the SA node pacemaker
practice.rationale: The LAD feeds most of the left ventricle — "the biggest engine part of your heart" — which is why a whole-LAD block is the widowmaker. The lateral LV and left atrium are circumflex territory, and the right ventricle is RCA territory.

practice.stem: Which receptor mediates sympathetic increases in heart rate and contractility?
options: Muscarinic receptors, stimulated by acetylcholine
Beta-1 receptors, stimulated by norepinephrine
Beta-1 receptors, stimulated by acetylcholine
Muscarinic receptors, stimulated by norepinephrine
practice.rationale: SNS: norepinephrine → β₁ → ↑ heart rate, conduction and contractility. Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine from the parasympathetic side and do the opposite: ↓ heart rate and AV nodal conduction.

practice.stem: Which statement about ejection fraction (EF) is accurate?
options: It is the total volume pumped out per minute, normally about 5 liters, measured by ECG
It is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, measured with a twelve-lead electrocardiogram
It is the volume of blood left in the ventricle after systole, measured by a lipid panel
It is the percentage of ventricular blood pumped out with each beat, measured by echocardiogram
practice.rationale: EF is "the percentage of blood that is pumped out of the ventricle with each beat," and "you need a echocardiogram in order to get this." About 5 L/min and HR × SV describe cardiac output, not EF.

practice.stem: The client's heart rate rises from 70 to 100/min while stroke volume falls from 70 mL to 35 mL. What happens to cardiac output?
options: It falls, from about 4.9 L/min to about 3.5 L/min
It rises, from about 4.9 L/min to about 7.0 L/min
It stays the same, because the two changes cancel out
It rises, because a faster heart rate always adds output
practice.rationale: CO = HR × SV — multiply, don't add: 70 × 70 mL ≈ 4.9 L/min becomes 100 × 35 mL = 3.5 L/min. A faster rate only raises output if stroke volume holds; you have to weigh both variables.

practice.stem: Which is the best description of preload?
options: Pressure the ventricle must overcome to open the aortic valve
Force of the ventricular squeeze during systole
Stretch of the ventricular muscle at the end of diastole
Volume of blood the ventricle pumps out each minute
practice.rationale: "Stretch is the word" — preload is ventricular stretch at end-diastole, set mostly by filling and venous return. Pressure to overcome is afterload, the force of the squeeze is contractility, and volume per minute is cardiac output.

practice.stem: Which statement best describes the Frank–Starling law of the heart?
options: More stretch always gives a stronger contraction, with no upper limit
More stretch gives a stronger contraction, but only up to a point
Contraction strength is set by hormones rather than by fiber stretch
More afterload gives a stronger contraction as the ventricle works harder
practice.rationale: "It's kind of like a rubber band. The further you stretch it out, the harder it bounces back" — and it "doesn't have to be regulated by any kinds of hormones." It works only up to a point: stretch too far and the cross-bridges no longer overlap enough to contract.

practice.stem: The client's blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. To open the aortic valve, the left ventricle must generate at least:
options: 91 mm Hg
121 mm Hg
241 mm Hg
151 mm Hg
practice.rationale: Afterload is set by the systemic pressure: at 120/80 "you have to create at least 121 millimeters of mercury" to open the aortic valve, and at 180 at least 181 — so 150 needs 151. 91 uses the diastolic number, and 121 is her normal-BP example.

practice.stem: The client has long-standing hypertension with widespread arteriolar vasoconstriction. What is the main effect on the left ventricle?
options: Afterload rises, so the ventricle must work harder to eject blood
Preload rises, so the ventricle stretches more and contracts harder
Afterload falls, so more blood leaves the ventricle with each beat
Contractility falls, because beta-1 receptors are being blocked
practice.rationale: Hypertension and vasoconstriction raise SVR, and ↑ afterload = ↑ cardiac workload — like pushing a door open "on a windy day… when the wind's coming back at you." That's why hypertension "is rough on the heart"; preload is about filling, not resistance.

practice.stem: The client loses a large volume of blood. Before any compensation kicks in, what happens?
options: Venous return falls, so preload rises and stroke volume increases
Preload falls, but stroke volume rises through the Frank–Starling law
Venous return and preload fall, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall
Afterload rises first, so stroke volume falls while preload is unchanged
practice.rationale: Less circulating volume means less blood returning to stretch the ventricle, so preload, stroke volume and CO drop (slide 27: ↓ circulating volume → ↓ CO). Frank–Starling works the other way here: less stretch gives a weaker contraction, not a stronger one.

practice.stem: The client's legs are raised, increasing venous return to a healthy heart. What happens initially?
options: Afterload rises → weaker contraction → stroke volume decreases
Preload rises → stronger contraction → stroke volume increases
Preload falls → heart rate rises → cardiac output stays the same
SVR rises → blood pressure rises → stroke volume decreases
practice.rationale: "If you put your legs up, you get more blood flow back to the heart" — more venous return means more stretch, a harder contraction and a bigger stroke volume (Frank–Starling). Venous return changes preload, not afterload or SVR directly.

practice.stem: Which vessels are the major determinant of the resistance blood meets in the systemic circulation?
options: Elastic arteries such as the aorta, which absorb the heart's pressure
Veins, which hold most of the blood volume as a large reservoir
Muscular arteries, which divert blood toward organs that need it
Arterioles, which are mostly smooth muscle and hugely numerous
practice.rationale: Arterioles are "teeny tiny tiny ones, but there's so many of them," so a little constriction there changes pressure a lot. Elastic arteries absorb pressure, veins are the reservoir, and muscular arteries redirect flow (e.g., fight or flight).

practice.stem: Plaque narrows the diameter of the client's artery. What happens to resistance and flow through that vessel?
options: Resistance falls and flow rises, like water through a big fat hose
Resistance rises and flow rises too, because pressure pushes blood through faster
Resistance rises and flow falls, like water forced through a tiny hose
Resistance is unchanged, because only blood viscosity sets resistance
practice.rationale: Smaller vessel = more resistance = decreased flow — "watering with a big fat hose versus a tiny hose." Diameter, length and viscosity all determine resistance, so viscosity is not the only factor.

practice.stem: Which equation did she give for blood pressure?
options: BP = cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance
BP = heart rate × stroke volume
BP = cardiac output + systemic vascular resistance
BP = stroke volume × systemic vascular resistance
practice.rationale: "Blood pressure is cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance," and cardiac output is its own equation, HR × SV. HR × SV alone is cardiac output, and it's a times, not a plus.

practice.stem: The client's heart is being repeatedly overstretched by volume overload. Which response helps counteract it?
options: Release of angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and veins
Release of aldosterone, which makes the kidneys retain sodium and water
Release of renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
Release of BNP and ANP, which promote diuresis and vasodilation
practice.rationale: Natriuretic peptides are released when the heart is stretched and "counteract volume overload" by promoting diuresis, dilating vessels and suppressing RAAS. Angiotensin II, aldosterone and renin are RAAS — "when at least the kidney thinks there isn't enough volume."

practice.stem: The client starts a drug that causes arteriolar vasodilation. Predict its effect.
options: SVR rises, so blood pressure and afterload rise
SVR falls, so blood pressure and afterload fall
Preload rises, so blood pressure and afterload rise
SVR falls, but afterload rises as the heart compensates
practice.rationale: Arteriolar vasodilation most directly decreases systemic vascular resistance (Kahoot), and with BP = CO × SVR, lower SVR means lower BP and less pressure for the ventricle to push against. Afterload follows SVR, so it can't rise when SVR falls.

practice.stem: The client starts a beta blocker. Using the blood pressure master equation, predict the main effect.
options: Heart rate falls, but SVR rises enough that blood pressure rises
Heart rate and contractility fall, so cardiac output and BP fall
Circulating volume falls, so preload and stroke volume fall
Arterioles dilate, so SVR falls while cardiac output is unchanged
practice.rationale: Slide 27 lists beta blockers under both ↓ heart rate and ↓ contractility — the CO side of BP = CO × SVR — consistent with blocking β₁ stimulation. Lowering circulating volume is the diuretic route, and vasodilation is the SVR route.

practice.stem: The client starts a diuretic. On the blood pressure master equation, which variable does it lower, and with what result?
options: Heart rate, lowering cardiac output and blood pressure
Contractility, lowering stroke volume and blood pressure
Circulating volume (preload), lowering cardiac output and BP
Arteriolar tone, lowering SVR and blood pressure
practice.rationale: Slide 27 places diuretics under ↓ circulating volume (preload) on the CO side: less volume → less preload → less CO → lower BP. Heart rate and contractility are lowered by beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine CCBs, and arteriolar tone by vasodilators.

practice.stem: Which sequence best describes atherosclerotic plaque formation?
options: Endothelial injury → inflammation/adhesion → LDL oxidation → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque
LDL oxidation → endothelial injury → fatty streak → foam cells → inflammation → fibrous plaque
Endothelial injury → foam cells → fibrous plaque → LDL oxidation → inflammation → fatty streak
Inflammation/adhesion → fatty streak → endothelial injury → foam cells → LDL oxidation → fibrous plaque
practice.rationale: "The very first thing, what starts atherosclerosis, is injury to the endothelial cells"; inflamed cells grow adhesion molecules, LDL is oxidized, macrophages engulf it to form foam cells, foam cells make a fatty streak, and collagen covers it as a fibrous plaque. Foam cells need oxidized LDL first, and the streak comes before the plaque.

practice.stem: In atherosclerosis, what is a foam cell?
options: A smooth muscle cell that has laid collagen over a fatty streak
A platelet that has stuck to tissue exposed by a ruptured plaque
An endothelial cell that has sprouted sticky adhesion molecules
A macrophage that has engulfed oxidized LDL within the intima
practice.rationale: Macrophages penetrate the intima and engulf oxidized LDL — "a combination of an immune cell, macrophages, as well as low-density lipoprotein, that creates a foam cell." Collagen-producing cells form the fibrous plaque, and adhesion molecules ("little sticky fingers") come from inflamed endothelium.

practice.stem: A plaque in the client's coronary artery ruptures. Why does this cause an acute myocardial infarction?
options: The plaque keeps growing slowly, narrowing the lumen a little more each year until it closes
Exposed tissue triggers platelets and clotting, and a thrombus suddenly blocks the artery
Pieces of the fibrous cap travel downstream and lodge in the cerebral arteries
Smooth muscle in the plaque goes into spasm and permanently closes the artery
practice.rationale: Rupture is like "ripping a scab off of a wound": the raw tissue underneath triggers platelet adhesion and clotting, and the clot can completely block an already-narrowed vessel. Slow growth narrows the lumen gradually; the sudden event is the thrombus. A coronary rupture causes ACS/MI, not a cerebral event, and the sources describe a clot — not smooth-muscle spasm — as what suddenly closes the vessel.

practice.stem: The client's atherosclerotic plaque ruptures in a cerebral artery. What is the expected consequence?
options: Ischemic stroke
Acute coronary syndrome
Acute limb ischemia
Hemorrhagic stroke
practice.rationale: "Where the plaque ruptures determines the consequence": coronary → ACS/MI, cerebral → ischemic stroke, peripheral → acute limb ischemia. A rupture makes a clot that blocks flow, so the stroke is ischemic, not hemorrhagic.

practice.stem: Which set matches the lipid targets she said you should know?
options: Total <240, LDL <130, HDL >40, triglycerides <200
Total <200, LDL <70, HDL >40, triglycerides <500
Total <200, LDL <100, HDL >60, triglycerides <150
Total <150, LDL <100, HDL >50, triglycerides <200
practice.rationale: "Our total cholesterol, we do want it to be less than 200. We want our LDL to be less than 100, our HDL to be greater than 60, and our triglycerides to be less than 150." LDL <70 is her post-MI goal, not the general target.

practice.stem: The client's lipid panel: total cholesterol 185, LDL 92, HDL 38, triglycerides 140 mg/dL. Which value is off target, and what did she call the best way to fix it?
options: LDL 92 — start a statin right away
Triglycerides 140 — start fenofibrate
HDL 38 — add niacin to raise it
HDL 38 — regular aerobic exercise
practice.rationale: Only HDL misses its target (>60), and "the best way that we have found to raise HDL is exercise." LDL 92 (<100) and triglycerides 140 (<150) are on target, and medications that raise HDL alone haven't consistently improved outcomes.

practice.stem: Which client is receiving secondary prevention for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)?
options: A client with diabetes and a high LDL but no prior events
A client with a prior ischemic stroke due to atherosclerosis
A client who smokes and has a family history of early MI
A client with hypertension and a borderline total cholesterol
practice.rationale: Secondary prevention prevents recurrent events in clients with established ASCVD — prior MI, ischemic stroke due to atherosclerosis or symptomatic PAD. Diabetes, smoking, hypertension and family history are risk factors; without an event, that's primary prevention.

practice.stem: After a heart attack, she said she wants the client's LDL to be below:
options: 70 mg/dL
100 mg/dL
130 mg/dL
150 mg/dL
practice.rationale: "If someone has already had a heart attack, we want their LDL to be below seventy, so we get a lot more aggressive." Below 100 is the general LDL target, and 150 is the triglyceride target.

practice.stem: A younger, otherwise healthy client has an LDL of 115 mg/dL and no other risk factors. What first step did she describe?
options: A high-intensity statin started at this visit, before any lifestyle trial
Ezetimibe alone as the first-line lipid-lowering drug for this client
About three months of lifestyle changes, then reassess
No action needed, because an LDL of 115 is already on target
practice.rationale: "If someone comes in and their LDL is one fifteen and they're younger and healthier… Let's do three months of lifestyle changes if you're willing." 115 is above the <100 target, high-intensity statins are for established ASCVD, and statins (not ezetimibe) are first-line.

practice.stem: The client's triglycerides are very high. Besides ASCVD risk, which complication is the concern?
options: Rhabdomyolysis
Acute limb ischemia
Liver damage
Acute pancreatitis
practice.rationale: Elevated triglycerides are linked to ASCVD, but "if you have really high triglyceride levels, we're also worried about pancreas." Rhabdomyolysis and liver damage are statin adverse effects, and acute limb ischemia comes from peripheral plaque rupture.

practice.stem: The client had an atherosclerotic MI last month. Which lipid strategy is generally indicated?
options: High-intensity or maximally tolerated statin, plus lifestyle changes
Three months of lifestyle changes before any lipid-lowering drug
A low-intensity statin to keep muscle side effects to a minimum
Fenofibrate as the first-line agent to bring the LDL down
practice.rationale: A prior MI is established ASCVD → secondary prevention: "we get a lot more aggressive with our high-intensity statins." Lifestyle-first is for the younger, healthier client in primary prevention, and fenofibrate targets triglycerides, not LDL.

practice.stem: How do statins lower LDL?
options: They block cholesterol absorption in the gut, so less dietary cholesterol reaches the blood
They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, so the liver makes less cholesterol and expresses more LDL receptors
They activate PPAR-alpha, so the liver clears more triglycerides out of the circulation
They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, so the liver makes less cholesterol and expresses fewer LDL receptors
practice.rationale: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → less hepatic synthesis → more LDL receptors → more LDL removed: "it also causes the liver to suck up some of the stuff that's in the bloodstream." Gut absorption is ezetimibe, PPAR-α is fenofibrate, and fewer receptors is the reversed direction.

practice.stem: A high-intensity statin is expected to lower LDL by about:
options: Less than 30%
50% or more
practice.rationale: High intensity = ≥50% LDL reduction; moderate = 30–49%; low = less than 30%. Only the percentages are fair game — "You don't need to know what doses are."

practice.stem: The client taking atorvastatin reports severe muscle pain and dark brown urine. What is the nurse's concern?
options: Myalgia — expected aching that settles if the client keeps taking it
Liver damage — the dark urine reflects statin-induced hepatotoxicity
Dehydration — concentrated urine because fluid intake has been low
Rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown products can damage the kidneys
practice.rationale: Severe muscle pain plus "Coca-Cola urine" is rhabdomyolysis: muscle contents are released and cause renal damage — the rare but serious effect she flagged for "lots of questions for exams." Plain myalgia doesn't darken the urine; the dark color is pigment from inside the muscle cells, not a sign of liver damage (that's checked with LFTs) or of low fluid intake.

practice.stem: The client on a statin is being evaluated for rhabdomyolysis. Which plan matches what she described?
options: Continue the statin and give an analgesic so the client can manage the aches at home
Stop the statin, admit the client, and give lots of fluids to protect the kidneys
Switch to fenofibrate and recheck a lipid panel in about three months
Hold the statin and restrict fluids to rest the injured kidneys
practice.rationale: "We want to stop this medication and usually… admit them to the hospital, lots of fluids, to flush all of these toxins out, and hopefully prevent long-term kidney damage." Restricting fluids works against flushing, and fenofibrate carries its own muscle toxicity risk.

practice.stem: The client starting a statin asks whether it will raise their risk of diabetes. Which response matches what she taught?
options: There is a slight increase in diabetes risk, but the heart benefits outweigh it
Statins have no effect at all on the client's chance of getting diabetes
The diabetes risk is high enough that at-risk clients should avoid statins
Statins lower blood sugar, so they actually help prevent type 2 diabetes
practice.rationale: "It does have a slight increase in diabetes rates, but all the other benefits are so amazing" that it's still worth it. So the risk is real (not zero) but small, and it doesn't make statins off-limits.

practice.stem: The client had an MI and takes a maximally tolerated statin, but the LDL is still above 70 mg/dL. Which add-on fits what she taught?
options: Fenofibrate, which increases triglyceride clearance
Niacin, the routine second-line drug for LDL
Ezetimibe, which blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption
A second statin added to double the LDL effect
practice.rationale: Ezetimibe (Zetia) is "usually combined with… a statin just to give us an extra boost" for additional LDL reduction. Fenofibrate is for severe hypertriglyceridemia, niacin is "rarely used routinely anymore," and the client is already on the maximally tolerated statin, so another statin isn't the add-on.

practice.stem: The client's LDL is at target, but the triglycerides are severely elevated (isolated hypertriglyceridemia). Which drug best fits?
options: A statin, the gold standard for every type of lipid problem
Ezetimibe (Zetia), which blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption
Niacin, the routine first choice for lowering triglycerides
Fenofibrate (Tricor), which increases triglyceride clearance
practice.rationale: Fenofibrate is "the one that's going to work really well against triglycerides." Statins are the gold standard except for isolated hypertriglyceridemia — "if your triglycerides are your only problem, statin is not the best choice" — ezetimibe targets LDL, and niacin is "rarely used routinely anymore."

practice.stem: The client takes atorvastatin, and fenofibrate is added for high triglycerides. What should the nurse monitor most closely?
options: Muscle symptoms and renal function, since muscle toxicity risk rises
Flushing and liver enzymes, since this pairing mainly causes flushing
Bleeding and bruising, since fenofibrate adds an antiplatelet effect
Nothing new, since fenofibrate is generally very well tolerated
practice.rationale: Fenofibrate: monitor renal function, and "there is more of a muscle toxicity risk if it's combined with the statins, so you've got to be careful with that." Flushing belongs to niacin, "generally well tolerated" describes ezetimibe, and fenofibrate's listed mechanism is triglyceride clearance, not an antiplatelet effect.

practice.stem: Shortly after taking a lipid-lowering drug, the client's face looks flushed and rosy. Which drug most likely caused this?
options: Ezetimibe
Niacin
Fenofibrate
Atorvastatin
practice.rationale: Niacin causes flushing (plus hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia) — her friend took a high dose to look "all flushed and rosy" and get sent home. Ezetimibe is generally well tolerated, fenofibrate's concerns are renal and muscle, and statins cause myalgia.

practice.stem: The client has high triglycerides, low HDL and high blood pressure; fasting glucose and waist circumference are normal. How should this be interpreted?
options: Does not meet the criteria, because hyperglycemia must be present
Does not meet the criteria, because at least 4 of the 5 are needed
Meets metabolic syndrome criteria, because 3 of the 5 are present
Meets the criteria only if the waist circumference is also enlarged
practice.rationale: Metabolic syndrome needs any three of five: high triglycerides, low HDL, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, large waist — "you need at least three of these criteria." No single criterion is mandatory.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Primary care clinic
clinical.setting: Primary care clinic · first visit to month 3
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0900 52-year-old male client here for an annual physical. No history of heart attack, stroke or peripheral arterial disease. Smokes 1 pack of cigarettes a day. His father had a heart attack at age 58. Works a desk job and “doesn't really exercise.” Eats fast food for lunch most days. Takes loratadine for seasonal allergies. Fasting lipid panel drawn last week. Vital Signs — T 36.7°C · HR 76 · BP 128/80 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Laboratory Results — Total cholesterol 246 mg/dL · LDL 168 mg/dL · HDL 38 mg/dL · Triglycerides 136 mg/dL Orders — Lifestyle counseling · provider to review statin therapy

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart. Which findings are risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease that need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: LDL 168 mg/dL
Triglycerides 136 mg/dL
Smokes 1 pack a day
HDL 38 mg/dL
Takes loratadine for allergies
Father's heart attack at 58
questions.rationale: Judge each lipid against the targets she said to know: TC < 200, LDL < 100, HDL > 60, TG < 150. LDL 168 is high and HDL 38 is low (dyslipidemia injures the endothelium); smoking injures the endothelium and lowers HDL; family history is one of slide 49's statin indications. TG 136 is under 150, and an allergy medicine plays no part.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the goal of treating this client's lipids?
options: Primary prevention — he has never had an ASCVD event
Secondary prevention — his father's MI counts as his established ASCVD
Secondary prevention — an LDL above 160 means he already has ASCVD
No prevention needed — his triglycerides and blood pressure are fine
questions.rationale: Primary prevention prevents the first ASCVD event; secondary prevention is for clients who already have established ASCVD — a prior MI, an ischemic stroke due to atherosclerosis or symptomatic PAD (slide 49). A family member's MI is a risk factor, not his own disease, and a high LDL is a risk factor, not an event. A normal TG doesn't cancel out a high LDL.

questions.stem: Which lab result is the main treatment target for lowering this client's risk of a heart attack or stroke?
options: HDL, because raising it with a drug is proven to prevent events
Triglycerides, because they are the main driver of plaque
LDL, because it is a major causal contributor to plaque
Total cholesterol, because only the total guides treatment
questions.rationale: Slide 47: “LDL is a major causal contributor to atherosclerosis. Lowering LDL reduces the risk of cardiovascular events” — she said LDL is “almost always the main goal.” Low HDL matters, but drugs that raise HDL alone haven't consistently improved outcomes (exercise is the best way to raise it). His TG is already under 150.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes moderate-intensity atorvastatin. Which items should the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Baseline liver enzymes before starting
Ezetimibe instead of the statin as the first-line drug
A follow-up lipid panel to check the response
Fenofibrate to bring his triglycerides down
Continued lifestyle changes alongside the statin
A drug to raise his HDL as the main treatment
questions.rationale: Slide 54: obtain a baseline lipid profile and liver enzymes, then monitor the lipid response after starting; lifestyle modification stays foundational (slide 49). Statins are first-line — ezetimibe is an add-on for extra LDL lowering; fenofibrate is for severe hypertriglyceridemia (his TG is under 150); HDL-raising drugs haven't consistently improved outcomes.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the client about atorvastatin and lifestyle changes. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Report severe muscle pain or urine that turns dark brown.”
“Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity.”
“Stop the statin if your legs ache a little after yard work.”
“Exercise is the best way we have to raise your HDL.”
“The statin works by blocking cholesterol absorption in your gut.”
“Quitting smoking lowers your risk by reducing damage to your vessels.”
questions.rationale: Teach the rhabdomyolysis warning signs — severe muscle pain and dark “Coca-Cola” urine. Slide 51: ≥ 150 min/week of moderate aerobic activity and smoking cessation (reduces endothelial injury); “the best way that we have found to raise HDL is exercise.” A little muscle aching can occur (“a little bit of muscle pain has been reported”) and is assessed, not a reason to stop on his own. Blocking gut absorption is ezetimibe; statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase in the liver.

questions.stem: Month 3, 0900. Repeat lipid panel: total cholesterol 178 mg/dL · LDL 94 mg/dL · HDL 44 mg/dL · TG 120 mg/dL. The client quit smoking 6 weeks ago and walks 30 minutes 5 days a week, but still eats fast food for lunch most days. He says he skips the statin “on days I eat healthy.” Which findings show the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: LDL 94 mg/dL
Still eats fast food for lunch most days
Quit smoking 6 weeks ago
Skips the statin on healthy-eating days
Total cholesterol 178 mg/dL
Walks 150 minutes a week
questions.rationale: LDL is now < 100 and TC < 200 — the targets she said to know — and quitting smoking plus 150 min/week of activity is the lifestyle plan in action. The fast-food lunches haven't changed — diet (less saturated and trans fat) is part of the plan, so that needs follow-up. Skipping doses needs follow-up: off the statin, levels “bounce back to where your higher level was, and then your risk factors go back up.”

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Cardiac step-down unit
clinical.setting: Cardiac step-down unit · hospital day 2 to week 6
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 2, 0800 58-year-old client admitted 2 days ago with an anterior wall MI. Cardiac catheterization showed a ruptured plaque with a thrombus in the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery. History of hypertension and type 2 diabetes; smokes ½ pack a day. Has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes acetaminophen as needed. Resting comfortably; asks, “How did this happen? I never had chest pain before.” Vital Signs — T 36.9°C · HR 78 · BP 132/80 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 97% on room air Laboratory Results — Echocardiogram: ejection fraction 40% · Total cholesterol 226 mg/dL · LDL 142 mg/dL · HDL 40 mg/dL · Triglycerides 168 mg/dL Orders — High-intensity atorvastatin daily · antiplatelet therapy · smoking-cessation counseling · lifestyle teaching before discharge

questions.stem: Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Ejection fraction 40%
SpO₂ 97% on room air
LDL 142 mg/dL
Heart rate 78
Triglycerides 168 mg/dL
Smokes ½ pack a day
questions.rationale: She said a healthy EF is 55–70% — at 40%, infarcted muscle “dies and does not contract anymore.” LDL 142 is far above the < 70 she wants after an MI, TG 168 is above 150, and smoking keeps injuring the endothelium. HR 78 and SpO₂ 97% need no follow-up.

questions.stem: The client asks how a plaque he never felt caused a heart attack. Put the steps in order, from the first event to the MI.
options: Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL, forming foam cells and a fatty streak
The plaque ruptures; platelets adhere and a thrombus blocks the LAD
Smoking, hypertension and diabetes injure the endothelium
Smooth muscle proliferates and collagen covers the streak as a fibrous plaque
questions.rationale: Slides 37–40: endothelial injury → inflammation, adhesion molecules (“little sticky fingers”) and LDL oxidation → macrophages engulf oxidized LDL (foam cells) → fatty streak → smooth muscle + collagen form a fibrous plaque (“a scab over a wound”) → rupture (“ripping a scab off”) → platelet adhesion, clotting cascade, thrombus → infarction. Most plaques never rupture, which is why there may be no warning.

questions.stem: The cardiologist called the client's blocked LAD the “widowmaker.” The client is most likely experiencing which injury?
options: Damage to the right ventricle, which pumps blood to the lungs
Damage confined to the lateral LV wall and the left atrium
Damage limited to one small, downstream coronary branch
Damage to much of the left ventricle, the heart's main pump
questions.rationale: Slide 9: the LAD supplies the anterior left ventricle and anterior septum — “the biggest engine part of your heart,” so a full LAD blockage is very hard to survive. The right ventricle is RCA territory, the lateral LV and left atrium are circumflex territory, and a small-branch block is the less severe situation she contrasted with a whole-LAD block.

questions.stem: Which items should the nurse anticipate in the client's secondary-prevention plan? Select all that apply.
options: An LDL goal below 70
Three months of lifestyle changes before any statin is started
High-intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy
Additional LDL-lowering drugs if the goal isn't reached
Low-intensity statin to avoid raising his diabetes risk
Smoking cessation
questions.rationale: After an MI he has established ASCVD: slide 49 calls for high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy, with additional LDL-lowering drugs if needed, and she wants LDL “below seventy.” Smoking cessation reduces endothelial injury. A lifestyle-only trial fits a younger, healthier client in primary prevention (her LDL 115 example); the slight diabetes risk is outweighed by the cardiovascular benefit.

questions.stem: Day 3, 1000. The client says, “The atorvastatin is the strong kind? My LDL is only 142.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Everyone's goal is an LDL under 100, so you need about a 30% drop.”
“After a heart attack the goal is under 70; this lowers LDL by 50% or more.”
“The high intensity is mostly to raise your HDL above 60.”
“You'll only need the strong dose until the artery has fully healed after the MI.”
questions.rationale: After an MI “we want their LDL to be below seventy, so we get a lot more aggressive,” and high-intensity statins lower LDL by ≥ 50% (moderate 30–49%). Under 100 is the general target, not the post-MI goal; statins don't do much for HDL (“we don't really have anything else for HDL”); and therapy is long-term, not until healing.

questions.stem: Week 6, 1400. Follow-up visit: LDL 66 mg/dL, no muscle pain, walking daily, no cigarettes since discharge. Which statement shows the client needs more teaching?
options: “If I get bad muscle pain and dark urine, I'll call right away.”
“Walking every day and not smoking help my arteries too.”
“My LDL is under 70 now, so I can stop the atorvastatin.”
“If I stop the statin, my LDL will probably climb back up.”
questions.rationale: Reaching the goal means the drug is working, not that it's done: stopping makes levels “bounce back to where your higher level was,” and she said it's likely lifelong. Reporting severe muscle pain with dark urine, keeping up exercise and staying smoke-free are all correct.

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Cardiology clinic
clinical.setting: Cardiology clinic and medical unit · days 1–12
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1000 70-year-old female client with a prior MI, on high-intensity atorvastatin for 8 months. Here for a routine follow-up. Reports “achy” thighs for about a week since starting a water-aerobics class; can still climb stairs and do her usual activities. Urine is light yellow. Wears bilateral hearing aids. Takes atorvastatin every evening without missed doses. Vital Signs — T 36.8°C · HR 72 · BP 126/76 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Laboratory Results — LDL 64 mg/dL · liver enzymes within normal limits Orders — Continue atorvastatin · assess muscle symptoms at each contact

questions.stem: Which findings are relevant to assessing this client for a statin adverse effect? Select all that apply.
options: Thigh aching for a week
Urine is light yellow
Can still climb stairs
Wears bilateral hearing aids
LDL 64 mg/dL
questions.rationale: Slide 54: assess for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, and dark urine. The aching is the cue; normal urine color and normal strength are pertinent negatives that help separate myalgia from rhabdomyolysis. LDL 64 shows the statin is working; hearing aids and BP have nothing to do with statin adverse effects.

questions.stem: The Day 1 findings are most consistent with which condition?
options: Rhabdomyolysis, which requires stopping the statin today
Statin myalgia — aching muscles without dark urine
Statin liver damage causing referred pain to the thighs
Muscle toxicity from combining a statin with fenofibrate
questions.rationale: “Myalgia may occur. So myalgia is aching muscles.” Rhabdomyolysis is severe muscle pain plus dark “Coca-Cola” urine — not present. Her liver enzymes are normal, and she isn't on fenofibrate (that combination raises muscle-toxicity risk).

questions.stem: Day 9, 0730. The client calls the clinic: her thighs are now so painful and weak she can't get out of a chair, and her urine is “dark brown, like cola.” The client is most likely experiencing:
options: Rhabdomyolysis from atorvastatin
Expected myalgia made worse by exercise
Liver damage from the atorvastatin
Dehydration from her exercise class
questions.rationale: Severe muscle pain with dark “Coca-Cola” urine is rhabdomyolysis — the rare but serious statin effect with “lots of questions for exams.” Myalgia is aching without dark urine; liver damage is picked up with liver function tests; the dark color here is pigment from broken-down muscle cells passing through the kidneys.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Stop the atorvastatin
Prompt evaluation for rhabdomyolysis
Hospital admission for lots of fluids
Restrict fluids to protect the kidneys
Switch to a higher-intensity statin
Continue the statin at a lower dose
questions.rationale: Slide 54: severe muscle symptoms or dark urine warrant prompt evaluation for rhabdomyolysis. She said “we want to stop this medication and usually… admit them to the hospital, lots of fluids, to flush all of these toxins out, and hopefully prevent long-term kidney damage.” Restricting fluids does the opposite, and any statin — higher or lower dose — keeps the cause going.

questions.stem: Day 9, 1300. The client is admitted and asks, “Why are you worried about my kidneys when it's my legs that hurt?” Put the events the nurse explains in order.
options: Lots of IV fluids flush the toxins out to prevent long-term kidney damage
Muscle cells break down
The released contents reach the kidneys and damage them (dark urine)
The cells' internal contents are released into the bloodstream
questions.rationale: “Rhabdomyolysis occurs when muscle tissue is broken down, and a whole bunch of the internal contents of muscle cells are released into the bloodstream. This will cause renal damage” — the “Coca-Cola urine” is pigment from the muscle cells passing through the kidneys. Treatment comes last: “lots of fluids, to flush all of these toxins out, and hopefully prevent long-term kidney damage.”

questions.stem: Day 12, 0900. After 3 days of IV fluids, the nurse reviews the client's progress. Which findings show the treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: Urine is light yellow again
Thigh pain 2/10, down from 9/10
Asks to restart atorvastatin at home tonight
Walks to the bathroom without help
Reports new aching in both shoulders
questions.rationale: Clearing urine, less pain and returning strength show the muscle breakdown is settling and the kidneys are being flushed. New muscle pain needs follow-up. Restarting the statin on her own isn't safe — it was stopped for rhabdomyolysis, and she noted some people who have had rhabdo “cannot take statins” any longer.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1500 68-year-old female client brought in by her daughter after 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea; has kept down only sips of water. Feels lightheaded when she sits up. Has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine; takes a moderate-intensity statin for hyperlipidemia. Echocardiogram last year: ejection fraction 60%. Lungs clear. Vital Signs — T 37.4°C · HR 122 · BP 86/52 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 97% on room air Laboratory Results — Liver enzymes within normal limits Orders — IV fluid bolus · vital signs every 15 minutes

questions.stem: Which findings are relevant to a fall in this client's cardiac output? Select all that apply.
options: 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea
Ejection fraction 60% last year
Heart rate 122
SpO₂ 97% on room air
Blood pressure 86/52
Takes levothyroxine
questions.rationale: Fluid loss with almost no intake drops circulating volume; the low BP is the result and the fast HR is the reflex response. An EF of 60% is in her healthy 55–70% range, so the pump itself was working; SpO₂ 97% and levothyroxine aren't part of this problem.

questions.stem: Put the chain that explains this client's low blood pressure in order.
options: Less stretch produces a smaller stroke volume
Cardiac output falls (CO = HR × SV)
Lost volume reduces venous return and preload
Blood pressure falls (BP = CO × SVR)
questions.rationale: Preload = stretch, set largely by venous return/volume. By Frank–Starling, less stretch → less forceful contraction → smaller SV; CO = HR × SV, and BP = CO × SVR. Slide 27 lists circulating volume (preload) as one of the levers on the CO side.

questions.stem: The heart rate of 122 shows the client is most likely experiencing which response?
options: Parasympathetic ACh on muscarinic receptors speeding the SA node
Natriuretic peptides released because the heart is overstretched
Aldosterone acting directly on the SA node within seconds
Baroreceptor reflex: SNS norepinephrine on β₁ to restore BP
questions.rationale: Baroreceptors are the “pressure sensor”: a drop in BP triggers reflex tachycardia within seconds to minutes through SNS NE → β₁ (↑ HR, conduction, contractility). ACh on muscarinic receptors slows the heart; natriuretic peptides answer volume overload (the opposite problem); aldosterone acts on the kidneys over days.

questions.stem: Which items should the nurse anticipate in this client's plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Restore circulating volume with the ordered IV fluid
A diuretic to clear extra fluid
Limit IV fluid to avoid stretching the heart
A beta blocker to slow the heart rate
Trend HR and BP every 15 minutes
An arteriolar vasodilator to improve flow
questions.rationale: Restoring volume raises venous return and preload, so SV and CO rise (slide 29: fluid retained → venous return ↑ → CO ↑), and the ordered vital signs track the response. A healthy heart (EF 60%) handles more filling — Frank–Starling. Slide 27's drug classes go the wrong way here: diuretics cut volume, beta blockers cut HR and contractility (removing her compensation), and vasodilators drop SVR — each lowers BP.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1600. The client has made very little urine since arrival. The daughter asks why. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Natriuretic peptides from her heart are telling her kidneys to hold on to water.”
“Her thicker blood has permanently damaged her kidneys.”
“Her kidneys sensed the low pressure and are holding on to salt and water.”
“Her parasympathetic system is slowing blood flow to her kidneys.”
questions.rationale: RAAS: “any drop in blood pressure or drop in fluid volume will be sensed by the kidneys” → renin → angiotensin I → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) → aldosterone, which tells the kidneys to “hold on to some water, hold on to some salt.” Natriuretic peptides do the opposite — they promote diuresis in volume overload. Dehydration does make blood more viscous, which slows flow, but nothing here shows permanent kidney damage. The parasympathetic system slows the heart; it isn't what's holding back urine here.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1900. After the fluid bolus: HR 94 · BP 112/70 · SpO₂ 97% · no longer lightheaded sitting up · urine output increasing · vomited once more an hour ago. Which findings show the treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: HR down from 122 to 94
BP up from 86/52 to 112/70
SpO₂ 97% on room air
No longer lightheaded sitting up
Urine output increasing
Vomited once more an hour ago
questions.rationale: As volume returns, preload, SV and CO rise, BP recovers, and the baroreceptor reflex no longer has to drive the heart rate up; the kidneys no longer need to hold on to as much water. SpO₂ was normal from the start, so it doesn't measure this plan, and more vomiting is ongoing volume loss that needs follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Internal medicine clinic
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Week 0, 1100 56-year-old male client here for a third blood pressure check. Readings at the last two visits were 162/96 and 166/98. Has gained 35 lb over the last 3 years. Takes no medications. Plays guitar in a weekend band. Recent echocardiogram: ejection fraction 62%. Vital Signs — T 36.6°C · HR 80 · BP 168/98 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 99% on room air Laboratory Results — Total cholesterol 184 mg/dL · LDL 88 mg/dL · HDL 62 mg/dL · Triglycerides 118 mg/dL Orders — Provider to start antihypertensive therapy · weight-management counseling

questions.stem: Which findings are relevant to the client's elevated blood pressure? Select all that apply.
options: BP 168/98 today
LDL 88 mg/dL
35-lb weight gain
Ejection fraction 62%
Prior readings 162/96 and 166/98
HDL 62 mg/dL
questions.rationale: A high BP across three visits is the problem. The weight gain matters: the body grows new vessels to feed the extra tissue — “more miles of blood vessels” — which raises resistance. His lipids all meet the targets she said to know (LDL < 100, HDL > 60), and an EF of 62% is in the healthy 55–70% range.

questions.stem: Put in order the chain by which this client's hypertension increases the work of his heart.
options: Afterload rises: the LV must exceed aortic pressure to open the valve
Arterioles constrict
Left ventricular workload increases over time
Systemic vascular resistance rises
questions.rationale: Arterioles are “the major determinant of resistance,” so their constriction raises SVR. Afterload is the pressure the heart must overcome — at 168 systolic the LV must make at least 169 mm Hg to open the aortic valve (her 120 → 121, 180 → 181 example) — and ↑ SVR → ↑ LV workload. “Hypertension is rough on the heart.”

questions.stem: Which hemodynamic change is the main concern for this client's heart?
options: Decreased preload from too little venous return
Increased afterload from high systemic vascular resistance
Decreased contractility from a loss of β₁ stimulation
Increased preload stretching fibers past their optimal length
questions.rationale: His problem is pressure, not stretch: “afterload = pressure,” determined by SVR, and ↑ SVR → ↑ LV workload — like pushing a door open against the wind. Nothing in the chart suggests too little or too much venous return, and a normal EF (62%) argues against weak contractility.

questions.stem: The provider wants a drug that lowers BP mainly by vasodilation, decreasing SVR. Which drug classes should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Beta blockers
Direct vasodilators such as hydralazine
Diuretics
Aldosterone antagonists
Alpha-1 blockers
questions.rationale: Slide 27 (her preview of next week): SVR is lowered by vasodilation — direct vasodilators such as hydralazine, and alpha-1 blockers (block α₁ → vasodilation). Beta blockers work on the CO side (↓ HR and contractility), and diuretics and aldosterone antagonists reduce circulating volume (preload).

questions.stem: Week 0, 1130. The provider prescribes a beta blocker. Before the first dose, which assessment relates most directly to how this drug lowers blood pressure?
options: Heart rate
Daily weight trend
Baseline liver enzymes
Fasting blood glucose
questions.rationale: Slide 27: beta blockers lower CO by decreasing heart rate and contractility — they block the SNS NE → β₁ effect (slide 10) — so heart rate is the assessment tied to the mechanism. A weight trend fits a drug that changes circulating volume, and liver enzymes are a statin baseline; glucose isn't how this drug works.

questions.stem: Week 8, 1100. The client has taken the beta blocker for 8 weeks. Which finding best shows the drug is working as intended?
options: HR 64, but BP still unchanged at 168/98 mm Hg
BP 138/86, but HR has climbed to 104 from 80
Weight down 2 lb, BP still 168/98 at this visit
HR 64 and BP 138/86, down from 80 and 168/98
questions.rationale: CO = HR × SV and BP = CO × SVR: slowing the rate (and contractility) lowers CO, which lowers BP — so both should fall. A slower rate with no BP change hasn't met the goal, a rising HR is the opposite of β₁ blockade, and weight isn't how this drug works.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Endocrine clinic
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Week 0, 1330 47-year-old male client with type 2 diabetes referred for a lipid review. Drinks 4–5 beers most nights. Has taken moderate-intensity atorvastatin for 1 year for a high LDL. Waist circumference 42 in (above the cutoff for men). Reports occasional heartburn after spicy food. No abdominal pain today. Vital Signs — T 36.8°C · HR 84 · BP 138/88 (elevated at the last 3 visits) · RR 16 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Laboratory Results — Triglycerides 940 mg/dL (H) · HDL 34 mg/dL (L) · LDL 92 mg/dL · Fasting glucose 142 mg/dL (H) · Renal function within normal limits · TSH within normal limits Orders — Provider to review triglyceride therapy · lifestyle counseling

questions.stem: Which of the client's findings are components of metabolic syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Triglycerides 940 mg/dL (H)
LDL 92 mg/dL
HDL 34 mg/dL (L)
4–5 beers most nights
Fasting glucose 142 mg/dL (H)
Waist 42 in, above the cutoff
questions.rationale: The five components are high triglycerides, low HDL, hyperglycemia, hypertension and a large waist circumference — the cutoffs are FYI (“You don't need to memorize the numbers”), so go by the flags. LDL isn't one of the five (and 92 is under 100). Alcohol raises triglycerides but isn't a criterion itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about this client's metabolic syndrome is accurate?
options: He doesn't meet criteria, because his LDL is below 100
He meets criteria only when all five components are present
He meets criteria: at least 3 of the 5 components are present
He meets criteria because his triglycerides alone are so high
questions.rationale: Metabolic syndrome needs at least 3 of the 5 criteria; he has all five (high TG, low HDL, high glucose, high BP, large waist). The cluster signals higher risk of heart disease, stroke and diabetes. LDL isn't a criterion, all five aren't required, and one abnormal value isn't enough.

questions.stem: Which complication is the nurse most concerned about given these lab results?
options: Acute pancreatitis from the very high triglycerides
Rhabdomyolysis from his current statin
Liver damage from moderate-intensity atorvastatin
Hypothyroidism driving up his triglycerides
questions.rationale: Slides 50 and 58: severe hypertriglyceridemia increases the risk of acute pancreatitis — “if you have really high triglyceride levels, we're also worried about pancreas.” He has no muscle symptoms, nothing in the chart points to liver injury, and his TSH is normal.

questions.stem: Which items should the nurse anticipate in the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Limit alcohol intake
Fenofibrate to increase triglyceride clearance
A high-intensity statin as the main triglyceride treatment
Better control of his diabetes as a secondary cause
Niacin as the first-line triglyceride drug
Weight management and regular aerobic exercise
questions.rationale: Slide 50: lifestyle changes, management of secondary causes (diabetes is one, slide 48) and selected TG-lowering drugs. Limiting alcohol is “particularly important in hypertriglyceridemia.” Fenofibrate (activates PPAR-α, increasing TG clearance) is the drug for severe hypertriglyceridemia. Statins only modestly lower TG (“if your triglycerides are your only problem, statin is not the best choice”), and niacin is rarely used routinely.

questions.stem: Week 0, 1400. The provider adds fenofibrate to the atorvastatin. Which statements should the nurse include in teaching? Select all that apply.
options: “Report muscle pain, weakness or dark urine promptly.”
“Fenofibrate lowers LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption in the gut.”
“Your kidney function will be checked with blood tests.”
“Taking it with the statin raises the risk of muscle toxicity.”
“With fenofibrate, you can keep drinking the same amount of beer.”
“You can stop the atorvastatin once the fenofibrate is working.”
questions.rationale: Slide 55: fenofibrate — monitor renal function; muscle toxicity risk with statins (“you've got to be careful with that”), so teach the muscle and dark-urine warning signs. Blocking gut absorption is ezetimibe; limiting alcohol stays in the plan; and the statin still treats his LDL — it's the gold standard.

questions.stem: Week 12, 1330. Triglycerides 310 mg/dL · renal function within normal limits. Which finding requires prompt follow-up?
options: Triglycerides down from 940 to 310 mg/dL
New thigh weakness and darker urine for 2 days
Cut back from nightly beers to 2 beers on weekends only
Waist down from 42 to 40 inches
questions.rationale: Muscle weakness with dark urine in a client taking fenofibrate plus a statin points to muscle toxicity — severe muscle symptoms or dark urine warrant prompt evaluation for rhabdomyolysis. The falling TG, less alcohol and smaller waist show the plan is working.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Neurology follow-up clinic
clinical.setting: Neurology follow-up clinic · months 6–9 after a stroke
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Month 6, 1000 66-year-old female client seen 6 months after an ischemic stroke caused by an atherosclerotic plaque that ruptured in a cerebral artery. Mild residual weakness of the left hand; walks independently. Has taken high-intensity atorvastatin since the stroke but says she “runs out a few days most months” before refilling. Her provider's LDL goal is < 70. Enjoys gardening and volunteers at the library. Asks, “I feel fine now — can I stop the pill?” Vital Signs — T 36.7°C · HR 70 · BP 124/76 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Laboratory Results — LDL 104 mg/dL · HDL 64 mg/dL · Triglycerides 128 mg/dL · liver enzymes within normal limits Orders — Provider to review lipid therapy · repeat lipid panel in 3 months

questions.stem: Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: LDL 104 mg/dL
Runs out of atorvastatin a few days most months
HDL 64 mg/dL
Asks whether she can stop the statin
Triglycerides 128 mg/dL
questions.rationale: LDL 104 is above her provider's < 70 goal (and even above the general < 100). Running out and wanting to stop are adherence problems — off the statin, levels “bounce back.” HDL 64 (> 60) and TG 128 (< 150) meet the targets she said to know, and the BP isn't part of this problem.

questions.stem: Why does this client need secondary rather than primary prevention?
options: Her LDL above 100 automatically counts as established disease
Any stroke, whatever the cause, counts as an ASCVD event
Her left-hand weakness shows the plaque is still growing
Her stroke from atherosclerosis means established ASCVD
questions.rationale: Slide 49 lists ischemic stroke due to atherosclerosis — with prior MI and symptomatic PAD — as established ASCVD, so the goal is preventing a recurrent event. The atherosclerotic cause is what counts, not just any stroke. A high LDL is a risk factor, not an event, and residual weakness is damage from the stroke, not proof of plaque growth.

questions.stem: Which outcome is the nurse most focused on preventing for this client?
options: Pancreatitis from her triglyceride level
Rhabdomyolysis from her high-intensity statin
Another plaque rupture causing a stroke or MI
Diabetes caused by long-term statin use
questions.rationale: Secondary prevention aims to prevent recurrent ASCVD events, and where a plaque ruptures decides the outcome (coronary → MI, cerebral → ischemic stroke, peripheral → acute limb ischemia). Her TG is 128, she has no muscle symptoms, and the slight statin diabetes risk is outweighed by the benefit.

questions.stem: Month 6, 1030. The provider decides to intensify LDL-lowering therapy. Which items should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Add ezetimibe to the statin
Continue the high-intensity atorvastatin
Replace the statin with fenofibrate
Strategies to keep her from running out of pills
Stop the statin and rely on lifestyle changes alone
A repeat lipid panel to check the response
questions.rationale: Slide 49: in secondary prevention, additional LDL-lowering medications may be needed to reach goals; ezetimibe (Zetia) is usually combined with a statin “just to give us an extra boost.” Reinforce adherence and monitor the lipid response (slide 54). Fenofibrate is for severe hypertriglyceridemia, and dropping the statin removes the gold standard.

questions.stem: The client asks, “If I take both pills every day and keep gardening, can I stop them in a year?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Most people stay on them long term; stopping lets your LDL climb back.”
“Yes — once your LDL is under 70, both pills can be stopped.”
“You can stop the statin once the ezetimibe has had time to work.”
“If you exercise 150 minutes a week, you won't need either pill.”
questions.rationale: Off the statin “you're just gonna bounce back to where your higher level was, and then your risk factors go back up.” Tapering after big lifestyle changes is “very rare” — “sometimes genetics rules the day” — and she said it's likely lifelong. Ezetimibe is an add-on to the statin, not a replacement.

questions.stem: Month 9, 1000. Repeat LDL is 66 mg/dL. The client now uses a weekly pill organizer and refill reminders. Which findings show the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: LDL 66 mg/dL
Says ezetimibe “keeps my gut from absorbing cholesterol”
Plans to stop atorvastatin now that her LDL is low
Uses a pill organizer and refill reminders
Says ezetimibe has replaced the need for her statin
questions.rationale: LDL is now below her < 70 goal, she has a system for adherence, and she correctly explains ezetimibe's mechanism (inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption). Planning to stop the statin, or thinking ezetimibe replaces it, needs reteaching — ezetimibe is an add-on, and stopping lets levels bounce back.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Clinic, cardiac unit and pharmacy · one question each
clinical.text: Five clients, one question each. Read each stem on its own.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client taking rosuvastatin for a high LDL that runs in her family tells the nurse she and her partner plan to try for a baby this year. Which response is best?
options: “Keep taking it — statins are the gold standard in pregnancy too.”
“Let's talk with your provider; statins are usually stopped in pregnancy.”
“Switch to niacin on your own until after the baby is born.”
“Keep taking it, but cut the dose in half once you find out you're pregnant.”
questions.rationale: Slide 54: discuss pregnancy plans — statins are generally discontinued during pregnancy. If a client wants to become pregnant, it's “talking to the docs about what are our options and coming off the statins.” Switching or adjusting drugs on her own isn't the plan.

questions.stem: A client who had rhabdomyolysis on a statin is prescribed niacin. Which adverse effects should the nurse teach the client to watch for? Select all that apply.
options: Flushing
Low blood glucose
Liver damage (hepatotoxicity)
High blood glucose
Slow heart rate
questions.rationale: Slide 55: niacin — flushing, hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia, with limited outcome benefit, so it's rarely used routinely; it may be an option for people who had rhabdo and can't take statins. (Her story: a friend took a high dose to look “flushed and rosy” and get sent home.) It raises glucose rather than lowering it.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has a BNP much higher than at the last admission. The nurse understands that this means:
options: The RAAS is releasing BNP to hold on to sodium and water
BNP is worsening the failure by constricting the arterioles
The client needs BNP replacement to treat volume overload
The heart is more stretched and stressed — worse heart failure
questions.rationale: BNP is released when the heart is overstretched; it promotes diuresis and vasodilation and suppresses RAAS a little. It's too weak to use as a drug — “we use them, however, as markers”: BNP gets higher and higher the more the heart is stressed in heart failure. Holding on to sodium and water is RAAS (angiotensin II, aldosterone).

questions.stem: A client recovering from an MI asks when the heart muscle itself gets its blood supply. Which answer is correct?
options: During systole, when contraction pushes blood into the coronaries
Equally in systole and diastole, since coronary flow is constant
Mainly in diastole, when the relaxed muscle lets coronaries fill
Only at the moment the AV valves close as contraction begins
questions.rationale: Coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole: “During systole, the constriction of the heart kind of prevents blood flow from going through the coronary vessels. So it's during the relaxation that we actually get really good blood flow to the heart muscle.”

questions.stem: While listening to a client's heart, a student nurse asks which valves are open while the ventricles eject blood. Which answer is correct?
options: Aortic and pulmonic open; mitral and tricuspid closed
Mitral and tricuspid open; aortic and pulmonic closed
All four valves open so blood moves straight through
Mitral and aortic open; tricuspid and pulmonic closed
questions.rationale: Slide 8: during filling the AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) are open and the semilunar valves closed; during ejection the semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonic) are open and the AV valves closed. There's a short moment when both sets are closed as contraction starts — never all four open.

cards.front: Valves while the ventricles are filling
cards.back: AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) OPEN · semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonic) CLOSED

cards.front: Valves while blood is leaving the heart
cards.back: Semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonic) OPEN · AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) CLOSED
Right = tricuspid · left = mitral

cards.front: When does coronary perfusion mainly occur?
cards.back: Diastole — during systole the squeezing heart muscle 'kind of prevents blood flow' through the coronaries
Anterior left ventricle + anterior septum · the 'widowmaker': it supplies 'the biggest engine part of your heart'
Lateral left ventricle + portions of the left atrium (wraps toward the back of the heart)
Most of the right ventricle
The 'pacemaker' · innervated by the ANS · resting rate 60–100 bpm

cards.front: Sympathetic effect on the heart (transmitter → receptor → effect)
cards.back: NE → β₁ → ↑ HR, ↑ conduction, ↑ contractility

cards.front: Parasympathetic effect on the heart (transmitter → receptor → effect)
cards.back: ACh → muscarinic → ↓ HR and ↓ AV nodal conduction (vagus nerve)
Atrial depolarization
Ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization is hidden — the ventricular signal 'washes out' that reading)
Ventricular repolarization
CO = HR × SV — 'This is an equation!' (multiply — don't add)
About 5 L/min (an average — adults come in lots of sizes)
55–70% of the ventricle's blood pumped out per beat (measured by echocardiogram) · she said 55–70; the slide says 55–75
STRETCH ('STREEEETCHHHHH!!!') — ventricular stretch at end of diastole, set mostly by venous return/filling
More stretch → stronger contraction, up to a point · like a rubber band: 'the further you stretch it out, the harder it bounces back' — overstretch and the cross-bridges don't overlap
PRESSURE the ventricle must overcome to eject, set by SVR · BP 120/80 → LV must make at least 121 mm Hg to open the aortic valve; like pushing a door open on a windy day

cards.front: Healthy heart: first effect of increased venous return
cards.back: ↑ Preload → more stretch → harder contraction → ↑ stroke volume (Frank–Starling)
Hypervolemia, regurgitation of cardiac valves, heart failure
Hypertension, vasoconstriction (↑ SVR directly ↑ afterload) · ↑ afterload = ↑ cardiac workload
Aorta + large branches · pressure absorbers — smooth out the swing between systolic and diastolic

cards.front: Major site of resistance in the systemic circulation
cards.back: Arterioles — tiny but so many that a little constriction changes pressure a lot; often the drug target
Thin walls, little smooth muscle, larger diameter, valves for one-way flow · hold most of the blood (a big reservoir) · skeletal muscle helps push blood back

cards.front: Three determinants of resistance to blood flow
cards.back: Vessel diameter, vessel length, blood viscosity (dehydration → more viscous blood)

cards.front: Smaller vessel diameter → resistance and flow?
cards.back: ↑ Resistance, ↓ flow · 'a big fat hose versus a tiny hose'

cards.front: How does obesity raise BP through vessel length?
cards.back: New vessels grow (angiogenesis) to feed extra tissue — 'more miles of blood vessels'
BP = CO × SVR (and CO = HR × SV)
Fast — seconds to minutes · reflex tachycardia or bradycardia to restore BP
Potent vasoconstrictor of arterioles and veins → ↑ SVR, ↑ BP (works over hours)
Kidneys hold on to sodium and water → ↑ volume → ↑ BP (works over days)
Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) → diuresis, vasodilation, suppress RAAS
Marker of heart failure — released when the heart is overstretched; rises as HF worsens (not manipulated with drugs)
Skeletal muscle contraction, respiratory pump, venous valves, sympathetic venoconstriction · legs up → more return; deep breath → negative pressure pulls blood back
Systemic vascular resistance (SVR)
Arteriosclerosis = thickening/hardening of vessel walls · atherosclerosis = its most common form: lipid-laden macrophages in the wall → plaque
Injury to the endothelial cells
Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia (↑ LDL, ↓ HDL), autoimmunity · plus inflammation markers, infection, air pollution
'Little sticky fingers' that grab macrophages and other immune cells from the passing blood
A macrophage that has engulfed oxidized LDL · many together = a fatty streak
Growth factors → smooth muscle proliferation + collagen over the fatty streak · 'like a scab over a wound'

cards.front: Why does plaque rupture cause sudden occlusion?
cards.back: Like ripping the scab off — exposed tissue → platelet adhesion + clotting cascade → thrombus blocks the vessel → ischemia/infarction
Coronary → ACS/MI · cerebral → ischemic stroke · peripheral → acute limb ischemia
↓ LDL → statins · ↓ platelet aggregation → antiplatelets · ↓ thrombus → anticoagulants · dissolve acute clot → thrombolytics
Cell membranes, steroid hormone synthesis, bile acid production
LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues (high LDL promotes atherosclerosis) · HDL does reverse cholesterol transport (higher is protective)
Transports triglycerides from the liver to peripheral tissues

cards.front: Ideal lipid values (the row she said to know)
cards.back: Total cholesterol < 200 · LDL < 100 · HDL > 60 · triglycerides < 150
Exercise — 'the best way that we have found to raise HDL is exercise'

cards.front: Very high triglycerides raise the risk of…
cards.back: Pancreatitis (plus ASCVD risk)
Prevent the first ASCVD event · lifestyle is foundational; statins first-line drug when indicated

cards.front: Secondary prevention: who, and which statin approach?
cards.back: Established ASCVD (prior MI, ischemic stroke due to atherosclerosis, symptomatic PAD) → high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin

cards.front: LDL goal after a heart attack
cards.back: Below 70 — 'we get a lot more aggressive'
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ liver cholesterol synthesis → ↑ hepatic LDL receptors → ↑ LDL removal from blood
Big ↓ LDL, modest ↓ TG, ↓ MI/ischemic stroke/ASCVD events · gold standard for HLD — but not the best choice for isolated high TG

cards.front: Expected LDL reduction by statin intensity
cards.back: High ≥ 50% · moderate 30–49% · low < 30% ('You don't need to know what doses are')

cards.front: Rhabdomyolysis on a statin — what and what sign?
cards.back: Rare but serious muscle breakdown; contents damage kidneys · severe muscle pain + 'Coca-Cola urine' (dark brown)
Stop the statin, prompt evaluation — usually admitted for lots of fluids to flush toxins and protect the kidneys

Generally discontinued during pregnancy — discuss pregnancy plans

cards.back: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (activates PPAR-α → ↑ TG clearance) · muscle toxicity risk with statins; monitor renal function

cards.front: Metabolic syndrome: how many criteria, and which five?
cards.back: At least 3 of 5: high TG, low HDL, high fasting blood sugar, hypertension, large waist · ↑ risk of heart disease, stroke, DM

qa.q: (student asked) A classmate's young relative died suddenly of an LAD heart attack — what causes that? Is it genetic?
qa.a: Probably a genetic predisposition to developing atherosclerosis sooner, unless something else was going on. "You have plaques in your body" — they're found from about age 3. Most never rupture, but a rupture is what causes a heart attack like that.

qa.q: (student asked) Could you repeat what you said about the LAD?
qa.a: The LAD supplies so much of the blood to the left ventricle, the part doing most of the work. A block of the whole vessel is very hard to survive (the "widowmaker"); a block in a smaller branch is a better situation.

qa.q: (student asked) What makes more blood come back to stretch the ventricle? (question partly inaudible)
qa.a: "A big determinant of that is the venous return." More venous constriction pushes blood forward, and a healthy heart compensates by pumping more.

qa.q: (student asked) How does vessel length affect resistance?
qa.a: Her example was obesity: the body makes new vessels to feed the extra tissue, so "you have more miles of blood vessels in your body," which on its own raises blood pressure.

qa.q: (student asked) So do taller people have higher blood pressure?
qa.a: Not a correlation. "It doesn't seem to have as much of an effect as long as you're healthy otherwise" — a taller person's heart compensates.

qa.q: (student asked) Does the body actually grow new vessels for the extra tissue?
qa.a: Yes — angiogenesis is "the fancy name for new blood vessel growth," and many things can cause it.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which equation correctly describes cardiac output?
qa.a: Heart rate × stroke volume — "Heart rate times stroke volume… There you go." (Multiply, don't add.)

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the best description of preload?
qa.a: "Stretch is the word."

qa.q: (Kahoot) What happens initially when venous return increases in a healthy heart?
qa.a: More blood coming back = ↑ preload → more stretch → contracts harder → stroke volume goes up (Frank–Starling). "It's a little tricky" — she said she would have accepted both the stroke-volume and the cardiac-output answer.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which change directly increases left ventricular afterload?
qa.a: Increased systemic vascular resistance. Decreased volume usually decreases afterload; increased venous return raises preload, which affects afterload only indirectly.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which receptor mediates sympathetic increases in heart rate and contractility?
qa.a: β₁ (answer not audible — from slide 10: NE → β₁ → ↑ HR, conduction and contractility).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Arteriolar vasodilation — which variable does it most directly decrease?
qa.a: Systemic vascular resistance. Arterioles are the major determinant of resistance.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which response helps counteract volume overload?
qa.a: Release of natriuretic peptides (ANP/BNP). Angiotensin II and aldosterone are RAAS — "that's going to be when at least the kidney thinks there isn't enough volume."

qa.q: (student asked) Is atherosclerosis an autoimmune disease?
qa.a: No. "It is chronic inflammation," but it isn't recognizing anything as foreign. Western diets and sedentary lifestyles drive a lot of it (she contrasted the "blue zones").

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which sequence best describes atherosclerotic plaque formation?
qa.a: Endothelial injury → inflammation/adhesion molecules → LDL oxidation → macrophages engulf oxidized LDL (foam cells) → fatty streak → smooth muscle + collagen → fibrous plaque (answer not audible — from slides 37–39).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why did that rupture cause an acute myocardial infarction?
qa.a: The rupture exposed the underlying tissue → platelet adhesion + clotting cascade → a thrombus suddenly occluded the coronary artery → ischemia and infarction (answer not audible — from slide 40).

qa.q: (student asked) How do you decide when to start a statin versus trying lifestyle first? (question partly inaudible)
qa.a: It depends on risk factors. After a heart attack she wants LDL below 70, so treatment is aggressive. A younger, healthier person with an LDL of 115 might get three months of lifestyle changes first, if willing.

qa.q: (student asked) What happens if someone stops their statin?
qa.a: Without other lifestyle changes, "you're just gonna bounce back to where your higher level was, and then your risk factors go back up."

qa.q: (student asked) If someone is young and healthy and it's genetic, should they be on a statin even so?
qa.a: "Once those numbers start going up," yes. Some people "do everything right and the genetics is so far against you" — "luckily we have things like statins."

qa.q: (student asked) Do statins make diabetes harder to control?
qa.a: Statins carry a slight increase in diabetes rates, but the other benefits are so large that it's still worth it. She wasn't sure about blood-sugar control itself — "that is a good question."

qa.q: (student asked) Is that gold standard for HDL or for HLD?
qa.a: HLD — hyperlipidemia. Statins are the gold standard for pretty much everything except isolated high triglycerides; "we don't really have anything else for HDL."

qa.q: (student asked) If you fix your lifestyle, you still can't come off the statin?
qa.a: "Very rare." Some people change enough to try tapering, but "sometimes genetics rules the day," and most adults don't make changes that drastic.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which treatment strategy is most appropriate after an atherosclerotic MI? (only "Which … strategy" was audible — question reconstructed)
qa.a: Secondary prevention: a high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin, plus lifestyle; more LDL-lowering drugs if needed (answer not audible — from slide 49).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A patient taking atorvastatin reports severe muscle pain and dark urine. What is the concern?
qa.a: Rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown releases cell contents that damage the kidneys ("Coca-Cola urine"). Prompt evaluation (slides 52, 54), and she said at 01:01:42 "we want to stop this medication" (the poll answer itself wasn't audible).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which medication lowers LDL by reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption?
qa.a: Ezetimibe (Zetia) (answer not audible — from slide 55).
